sentences.text: Listen to a podcast interview with Philip, Charles and Anna, who are talking about their experiences as language learners.
Complete the information in the spaces below.
You now have 30 seconds to study the task.
At the end of the task, you will have one minute to tidy up your answers.

Philip, Charles, Anna, many thanks for joining me on today's language learning podcast, in which we're going to discuss the topic of heritage language learning, First of all, and for all our listeners who may not
know what this means, can you tell us, Philip what is heritage language learning?
It’s great to be here, thanks.
So, I think I think we all know what language learning is.
is. For example, we learn languages at school, from our friends from other countries, or because we need another language for work.
Heritage language learning is a little bit different.
Yeah, it’s different because it means we're all learning languages that are strongly connected to our cultural backgrounds.
I see. So, unlike those who just learn a language language for work or because they’re forced to, you’re all learning a language from your cultural background.
In other words, your heritage.
Charles, is that how you understand it?
Yeah, that’s right.
Like, my family migrated to the U .S.
from Peru a hundred years ago in the 1920s, so that’s why I’m learning Spanish.
Yeah, I mean, I suppose I’m quite similar to Charles, but my family migrated to England England, rather than the USA in the 1960s.
They’re a Chinese family from Singapore originally and so that’s why I'm learning Mandarin.
So, Charles is learning Spanish.
Anna, you're learning Mandarin.
And Philip, how about you?
What language are you learning?
My family are originally from southern Belgium, before they moved to Yorkshire in the North of England.
So, I am learning French.
OK, the south of Belgium so French.
Can I ask then, apart from the strong cultural connection you have, what are some of the other reasons you have for learning your heritage language?
Philip, can I start with you?
Sure. Well for me, I was asked to give a speech at my cousin’s wedding in Belgium.
I mean, I learned French at school in England and everything, but I didn’t think that was enough.
So, I needed to improve my speaking and grammar for the big day.
Ah, I see, so you needed to impress all your relatives at the wedding!
How about you, Charles?
Well, I wanted to explore my identity.
We all know that language is connected to identity, so I wanted to explore my Peruvian identity through learning Spanish.
I guess that’s the same for others, is it?
for me, it wasn’t really about identity, but it was more for speaking with my grandparents back in Singapore.
I want to be able to speak Mandarin with them so I can get to know them better.
So, by learning Mandarin you can chat with your grandparents sounds like a good reason to me.
Oh, I almost forgot.
How have you all been learning?
I mean, what methods have you mainly been using?
Anna? I found a language exchange partner where I live, who speaks to me in Mandarin.
OK, a language exchange partner seems like a good way to learn.
How about you Philip?
I've been learning French with a textbook.
This works well for me because I want to learn lots of grammar and vocabulary.
Plus, I quite like learning on my own.
A textbook huh?
I hope you’ve found a good one.
Charles, what methods have you been using?
Well, I have lessons every week with a private tutor.
It’s expensive, but she’s a really, really good teacher.
so I’m pretty happy with that.
Every week with a private tutor?
You must be speaking like a native by now!
OK, so moving on to the next question.
What are some of the difficulties you’ve found when learning your heritage language as an adult?
Let’s stay with Charles.
Well, for me, I’d say the greatest difficulty is learning all of vocabulary there are still so many words I don’t know.
But I’m trying to improve by using a language learning app on my way to work.
Anna? I use an app as well to help me learn new words, but the biggest problem I have is with reading and writing Chinese characters.
So, I really need to practice every day, and and I do that by writing a daily diary in Chinese.
Thats a great idea.
I'm sure by writing your thoughts down in your diary every day you can really learn those Chinese characters in no time.
How about you Philip?
My difficulty is a bit different from the others and it’s to do with listening.
No one in my family speaks much French, so I can’t practice my listening with them.
Luckily, though, I found a really good YouTube series in French, which I watch every week.
It helps me to hear, like, the natural rhythms of the language.
YouTube’s really useful for language learners, isn’t it?
Yes, but you have to watch it regularly, like every week.
Otherwise it’s not enough.
OK, so my final question is: what message would you have for those who are thinking of learning a heritage language?
Charles? Well, I'd say, it’s never too late to learn.
I didn’t start until I was already in my thirties.
I mean, most people say it’s better to start young, but I disagree: I'm much better at learning Spanish as an adult than as a child.
How about you, Anna?
I agree with Charles, but I guess my message would be: motivation is everything.
Without Without motivation you'll never succeed.
Connecting with my Chinese heritage motivates me so much, not least being able to visit and talk with my relatives in Singapore.
Motivation is everything.
A strong and important message, Anna, thanks.
How about you Philip?
Hmm, that's a hard one.
I suppose my message would be there's not one right way of learning.
learning. It's hard learning a new language, especially if you haven't got much opportunity to practice.
I mean, you have to be ready to try out lots of new ways to learn, as well as what you've always done.
Good messages from you all and Philip hits the nail on the head, I think there's no single right way to learn a language, and we should all try out different ways to succeed.
Well, that’s about all we have time for today.
Today, join us next time for another exciting podcast.
